Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette:
Samira Haddad is an 80-year-old widowed Arab American social worker who came to treatment after years of trying to live around a loss she has never been able to settle inside herself. The event she returns to is her child's life-threatening illness, which unfolded largely in the hospital and is remembered less as a coherent story than as a series of unbearable moments pressed into her body. She describes long corridors washed in fluorescent light, the sharp antiseptic smell that clung to her clothes and hair, and the sight of needles, IV poles, and clear tubing surrounding her child's bed. At the time, she moved through those days as both mother and professional, speaking to doctors, asking questions, trying to sound calm. Yet what stays with her now is not confidence but the terrible sense of standing beside someone she loved while the machinery of treatment took over. She remembers being asked to consent, to wait, to hold herself together. What haunts her is the belief that in those moments she behaved in ways that violated the kind of mother she believed herself to be. She had always seen herself as protective, steadfast, and guided by deep family loyalty, and she has come to believe that she failed that standard in the most important moment of her life.

In the months and years that followed, memories did not come to her as orderly recollections. More often, they forced their way in without warning. She may be sitting quietly and suddenly feel the same crushing emotional intensity as if she were back in the hospital, but with no clear image attached to it. She describes it as grief arriving full force before her mind can even catch up, a wave of dread and sorrow that seems to come from nowhere and then leaves her shaken. When the memory does take shape, it is accompanied by overwhelming grief. She speaks of it as something she cannot touch for long; as soon as she begins to remember, she feels she may be swallowed by it.

Because of this, Samira has spent years trying to push the memories out of her mind. If thoughts begin, she redirects herself sharply, tells herself not to go there, turns on the television, starts tidying, or recites practical tasks to herself. She also narrowed her world. Going out began to feel risky, not because she feared the outside in general, but because the world seemed full of reminders she could not control. A passing ambulance, a clinic sign, a conversation in a waiting room, even the sterile smell in a pharmacy aisle could undo her. Over time she started declining invitations and limiting errands. As a widow, this shrinking of daily life has left her more isolated, though she speaks of it less as loneliness than as necessity: if she stays home, she is less likely to be caught off guard.

Her work as a social worker has made these collisions especially painful. For much of her life she was accustomed to listening to other people's suffering, but certain conversations became hard to bear. When clients or colleagues spoke about people losing loved ones, she felt herself tense immediately, as if the room had become unsafe. She could still hear the words, but inside she was no longer fully present; she was fighting the surge of feeling and trying not to let her mind go where it wanted to go. Medical settings were worse. She began avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations. The sight of needles or drips was enough to make her chest tighten and her thoughts scatter. She understood that these reactions made ordinary healthcare and parts of her professional life more difficult, but to her they felt like the only way to keep from being overwhelmed.

Alongside this, Samira has become convinced that the illness changed her permanently for the worse. She says she used to be stronger, more open, more able to face hard realities. Now she sees herself as diminished, someone marked by what happened. What frightens her most is not only the memory itself but the conviction that she has no protection against catastrophe. She is certain that bad things can happen without warning and that, when they do, she cannot stop them. That sense of helplessness sits heavily beneath her daily routines and makes even small decisions feel shadowed by danger.

She finally sought help after recognizing how much of her life had become organized around not being reminded. A recent encounter with the antiseptic smell in a medical office, followed by intense grief that stayed with her for days, left her shaken enough to admit that the problem was not passing with time. She says she wants, at her age, to be able to leave the house, attend to her health, and hear ordinary conversations about illness and loss without feeling ambushed. At the same time, she is afraid that if she stops pushing the memories away, the grief will be endless and she will find only more evidence that she failed when her child needed her most.
